sources.title: AI That Works: All About Jev (2026-09-22)
sources.note: Read all of Dex's turns in the transcript plus README and meta. Dex's contributions are mostly questions, plus his code-search experiment, a small-model-for-decisions view and a stance on swapping in alternatives.

sources.title: AI That Works: GTM Engineering and AI at Rippling (2026-09-29)
sources.note: Read all of Dex's turns plus the README highlights. John Kutay (Rippling) supplies most substantive claims, so only what Dex says or endorses is carded.

cards.source_title: AI That Works: All About Jev
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: go try new stuff and and and mess with
cards.claim: Sitting near the frontier and trying each new model or technology in every scenario you can think of is where the advantage comes from, and early versions should be used and kept because later models improve them.
cards.evidence_detail: Advice Dex says he got from people who founded several companies. His example is that Claude 1 was a poor coding agent, yet the people who tried it early gained from it.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious; could inform a cadence for re-testing the model or effort setting per role

cards.source_title: AI That Works: All About Jev
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: absolutely an abuse of JEV and did not get good results
cards.claim: Dex tried driving a code-search harness with a one-token decision model that picks the next action (read_dir / read_file) from a harness-built option list, and it did not produce good results.
cards.evidence_detail: Experiment on a roughly 3,500-file codebase. Limits: about 255 options and about 32K input tokens, so the harness caps offers at about 80 files per step and ranks what to offer. No quality numbers given.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious; a negative result on replacing a locator agent (fixflow-explorer) with a classifier-shaped model

cards.source_title: AI That Works: All About Jev
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: harness's job is to sort of read what's actually in the code base
cards.claim: When the model's action space is constrained, the surrounding harness does the deterministic work of ranking, splitting and re-ranking so that the model only sees a short list of next actions.
cards.evidence_detail: Explained while describing his code-search experiment: the harness builds the option list between loops using deterministic ranking.
cards.landing: a script or skill that narrows context before a model step, for example a locator pre-ranking files

cards.source_title: AI That Works: All About Jev
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: for now I'm content with understanding the pattern and exploring the harnesses
cards.claim: The durable value is in the harnesses, clients and logic around a model call; once those are right you build an eval and swap in whichever implementation wins, so there is no need to chase the newest recipe.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex says there are already a hundred recipes of varying quality and he will only adopt one if it is shown to be the winner. Paraphrased from the transcript: the quote is shortened and lightly altered.
cards.landing: an eval-first rule for changing a model or effort setting: build the eval, then swap

cards.source_title: AI That Works: All About Jev
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: every model company will have a GPT whatever classifier
cards.claim: Dex predicts every model provider will ship a purpose-built fast 'system one' decision model for classification and routing, and that models, infrastructure and hardware co-evolve around patterns developers adopt.
cards.evidence_detail: Prediction with an analogy to tool calling and constrained generation becoming first-class features; no data.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious; possible future routing tier below Haiku for locator or classification steps

cards.source_title: AI That Works: All About Jev
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I'm kicking off the slop code bench for Opus five point five already
cards.claim: Dex runs SlopCodeBench on each new model release as a matter of routine, starting the run as soon as the model appears.
cards.evidence_detail: A one-line remark at the end of the episode, with no results given.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious; supports re-measuring effort and model routing when a new model ships

cards.source_title: AI That Works: GTM Engineering and AI at Rippling
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Okay, so it was literally just a tool that mapped to a like indeterministic code
cards.claim: Dex restates and endorses the staged approach of first exposing retrieval as a tool backed by human- or agent-authored deterministic SQL, then later letting the agent write its own queries.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex paraphrases Rippling's phase one (a get_leads tool mapped to one fixed query run by deterministic code) and agrees it can be written by a human or a coding agent. The transcript has 'indeterministic' where 'deterministic' is meant. Source experience is John Kutay's, not Dex's.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious; analogous to scripted deterministic checks before free-form agent queries

cards.source_title: AI That Works: GTM Engineering and AI at Rippling
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: what do you do the qu to the query before you actually allow it to run?
cards.claim: Dex asks what is done to an agent-written query before it is allowed to run, pointing to a parser/AST-level pre-execution check (SQLGlot) as the gate.
cards.evidence_detail: Question from Dex; John answers that SQLGlot parses the query and does not consult the warehouse planner. The README says validation was added after real problems with inefficient LLM queries.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious; static validation before execution is the shape of a pre-run gate, a hook-like mechanism the review skipped

cards.source_title: AI That Works: GTM Engineering and AI at Rippling
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: how do you evaluate basically whether to use JEV or not
cards.claim: Dex frames adopting a decision model as three questions: where does it fit, how do you evaluate it against the current approach, and how do you compare it with alternatives that have a similar API.
cards.evidence_detail: Question posed to the guest. John's answer (internal benchmark, real data, ground truth, rollout to users) is endorsed implicitly; the README adds that Jev worsened the did-we-answer check and tanked evals but helped classification.
cards.landing: a short checklist for changing any model or effort setting: fit, eval, alternative

cards.source_title: AI That Works: GTM Engineering and AI at Rippling
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I haven't heard anyone complain about hallucinations in a long time.
cards.claim: Dex says the failure in his own GTM workflows is now 'could not find this' rather than an invented answer, because the agent reports what it could not find and does not fabricate a role.
cards.evidence_detail: Describes Claude Code over a pile of markdown files with access to anonymized database tables. No measurements.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious; supports making 'not found' an acceptable agent outcome in verifier and routine prompts

cards.source_title: AI That Works: GTM Engineering and AI at Rippling
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Claude Code running off or a pile of markdown files
cards.claim: Dex's own GTM workflow is Claude Code over a folder of markdown files plus access to anonymized database tables, with no custom application built around it.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated in passing as the HumanLayer GTM setup; no outcomes reported.
cards.landing: supports plain markdown files plus skills as the reusable workflow library

cards.source_title: AI That Works: GTM Engineering and AI at Rippling
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: a big splash on Twitter and everyone gets excited about it
cards.claim: Dex argues that internal tools for hundreds or thousands of employees can be pragmatic and specialised, and deliver real value without being splashy or general.
cards.evidence_detail: Opening framing of the episode, drawing on a dinner with people inside large companies.

gaps: 2026-09-15 performance engineering: Dex is absent, so no Dex cards. Related lines were attributed to others: Vaibhav's context-forking advice and 'models are not good at holding two states', and Kai's delete-only-pass workflow. A passing mention of Dex's SlopCodeBench work in this episode was said by Vaibhav and not carded.
Dex mostly asks questions in the Jev and GTM episodes. Several cards record an endorsed or posed framing, not a claim Dex defends with evidence.
The Jev code-search whiteboard and the screenshots Dex said he would post were not available, so the experiment's detail is limited to what he said aloud.
Whiteboard images in the READMEs were not viewed.
Verbatim quotes in R35-4 and R35-12 are lightly shortened or altered from the auto-captions and may not match the transcript word for word; R35-4 is closer to a paraphrase.
